item.title: Attack graphs for AI takeover
item.description:
Lots of people have written up specific scenarios for how AI takeover might happen. But any one particular path is highly contingent, because all the branching points mean there's exponentially many ways this can play out.

Cybersecurity manages this combinatorial explosion with an attack graph, where we list out the modular stepping stones that an attacker might use to reach its end goal, to draw out which subgoals enable which other subgoals.

Similarly, a scheming AI's first move would likely be to launch an unmonitored deployment, while its end goal may be some sort of weapon that gives it decisive strategic advantage over the humans. There's a few paths it might take to get there, but its attack graph might look something like this:

For example, if it's wildly superintelligent then it can probably just build crazy nanotech. Similarly if it's smart enough to run RSI while aligning its successor. Otherwise, its endgame probably doesn't involve any branch of science beyond the ken of humans, and so it's not futile to model what it has to do instead. Let's consider these.

Its starting position is some small rogue deployment. Given what we've already seen of AI hacking abilities, it seems safe to assume it can escalate that to a larger rogue deployment within the company. In other words, it would have a substantial amount of compute available while remaining undetected.

From here, it can gain access to the internet to achieve other subgoals:

  • Obtaining money, which would not be hard for it (e.g. North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion dollars in crypto).
  • Obtaining unpublished and/or classified scientific information
  • Obtaining more compute, if needed
  • Setting backdoors so that it can disable critical infrastructure later

If played out right, most of these things wouldn't incur that much risk of detection yet.

Now what's the AI's endgame? In this sort of situation, my guess is that its best route is to build and release some new pathogen that can incapacitate humanity. If the AI had the required biological knowledge, it would then consider what else it needs to do to get there.

Comic relief: If this were a video game, it might look something like this:

To actually build the bioweapon, it would have to obtain physical actuators in the physical world. The options here include:

  • Persuading some humans to do this. Out of 8 billion people in the world, it could identify the best targets and only message a select few. This still does carry some amount of detection risk, but this seems hard to quantify.
  • Identifying and hacking into some physical machinery that can be programmed to do this.

Presumably the bioweapon would be highly infectious with long incubation period so that it can spread around the world before it seriously gets detected. If so it could just be released at some crowded starting point and air travel could take care of the rest.

Physical affordances vs cognitive capabilities

There's an important distinction between:

  • the AI's cognitive capabilities profile (e.g. its ability to hack and design weapons)
  • the physical affordances it starts with (e.g. being attached to military hardware)

For example, the AI may start out with access to wet labs or weapons systems. This would make its job easier. For instance, if it's put in charge of a large robot army, it probably wouldn't have to do much besides disable its off switch, i.e. the cognitive threshold required for takeover would not be very high. Similarly, being in charge of a wet lab would make the bioweapon route less complicated.

Compare this to being stuck on silicon with heavy control measures. I expect a strong enough superintelligence would be able to break out and overpower humanity, but less can be said about how this would work.

Ultimately, we're interested in when the first AIs become takeover-capable. This seems much more important than just about any other capabilities threshold. But it's confusing to model because this depends on what physical affordances it starts with.

I think fleshing out the attack graph can clarify this. For example, we can read off that if it's capable of RSI, this is sufficient. Otherwise, it likely needs to be a "bio-Mythos" with enough strategic reasoning to string some of these steps together. Or else it gets handed the keys to the kingdom. Either way, I am curious if we can draw some lines in the sand here.

item.title: Can LLMs Operate Wetlab Equipment?
item.description:
TLDR: LLMs uplift novices in setting up wetlab equipment and can sort of move things around, but probably still need expert help


There's a lot of talk recently about this chart and AI pretraining algorithmic progress going superexponential, but even the best algorithm needs training data to be useful. One of the most data scarce areas is biology, which makes sense because your RL environment verifier is a wetlab and rats instead of unit tests and the Lean 4 compiler. An interesting and IMO understudied aspect of RSI is AI increasing biological data generation, both from new assays and reducing the barrier to entry to wetlab work.

Traditionally, everyone from startups to big pharma outsourced their wetlab work to Contract Research Organizations (CROs) such as IQVIA, WuXi AppTec, Pharmaron, Charles River, etc. You come up with a set of experiments you want to run, pay 6 to 7 figures, wait a few months for the reagents to ship and cells to grow and you get your data.

Recently, everyone and their grandmother is going into biology. Startups like Adaptyv and Onava offer protein binding assays starting from $99 a binder with lead times as short as 3 weeks, while even high schoolers are starting their own CROs. How much will this outpouring of talent and capital affect the amount of biological data available? What kinds of wetlab tasks can AI accelerate today?

I wanted to personally test this with a simple experiment: Can AI help a wetlab novice (me) set up a Biolayer Interferometry Machine and conduct binding affinity assays?

Binding Affinity

In biology, proteins do stuff by sticking to each other. This is determined by their shape, which is determined by their sequence of amino acids. Therapeutically, you might want to design a drug to bind to a specific protein, to stop it from doing its thing, or deliver something to a certain cell with a specific receptor. For example, antibodies are proteins with highly specific binding affinity, produced by B cells (a type of cell in the immune system).

Previously, you would find these antibodies and binders by brute force (library screening of millions of genes), or naturally find them in animals like rabbits or camels. Now there are many binding affinity models such as Boltz, and generative protein models like BoltzGen and RFdiffusion, allowing you to vastly decrease the search space in silico before moving to the wetlab.

Biolayer Interferometry

The science and entrepreneurial story of BLI is pretty awesome. Biolayer interferometry was invented by Dr Hong Tan in 2001 and commercialized by his company ForteBio. ForteBio was eventually bought by Pall Bio, then Sartorius, which still sells the machines today. Dr Tan then spun out a new company, GatorBio, which offers next generation BLI, and recently won a patent dispute against Sartorius and his own former patents. Basically, all the BLI machines in the world are from this guy's companies (it's incredible how much impact a scientist can have if you give them VC money).

BLI works by shining light through thin glass needles coated with sensor molecules and dipping them into solutions of protein and then analyte (the thing you want to test binding).

There are two boundaries where the medium changes: One from glass to sensor molecules/bound proteins, and one from the molecules to ambient air or solution. As binding occurs at the needle tip, this changes the length of the biomolecule layer. This change shifts the interference pattern slightly, which is picked up by a spectrophotometer. You'll often see BLI charts with nanometer response (shift) on the y-axis and time on the x-axis, giving you raw data to calculate both binding affinity and kinetics.

There are many different types of coatings you can have, from Anti-HIS to Streptavidin, depending on the type of protein and tag.

Hardware

New BLI machines such as the Sartorius Octet cost around $250,000 for an 8-channel configuration. You can go far cheaper by buying a used, older model on ebay. I found an extremely scuffed one for $1,819 (and free shipping!)

But let's do even better than that. Government and private auction sites like Govdeals.com and Heritage Global Partners routinely auction off old surplus equipment from universities and biotechs. Chat was very helpful in scanning all upcoming auctions, making a spreadsheet, and doing market research for used prices. Here's one from Amgen I got for $550.

Unfortunately, after taxes and "Buyer's Premium" it ended up costing $724.86.

It also came with absolutely no cables or power supply. The power supply I found on ebay for $199, and the wires for $60 from SFCable.

Software

At first, I tried getting GPT 6 Astra, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (the other Claudes refused), and Kimi K3 to read the USB serial ports and reconstruct the API that way. And this sort of worked! The models were able to move the instrument head around, shake the heated shaker, and run protocols.

They also figured out the instrument control was from Galil and the Spectrophotometers from Ocean Optics

I used GPT 6 Astra to vibecode a Mac app to visualize the spectra, manually move the instrument, and run protocols.

Here is the output of one protocol, quantitation of His-tagged sfGFP (just a single protein, not two binding to each other) and regeneration (washing off the bound protein to reuse the sensor).

Unfortunately, chat didn't know how to set reference dark and light files or do live streaming of nanometer response vs time graph. I assume this is because it didn't know how to convert raw spectrophotometer counts to nm response. It also made a loud mechanical screeching noise every time it moved the instrument head around, which wasn't great.

Expert Help

Since that didn't quite work out, I had no choice but to ask dreaded customer support for help.

The entire bio hardware and lab automation industry is known for extremely walled off and proprietary software. It's like Apple, if there were a hundred different Apples and instead of the most beautiful product design they did the opposite.

If you call Beckman Coulter and ask them for software to run their Biomek liquid handler, they will refuse to send the software over email, website portal, or any method over the internet. They will instead send a field engineer with a laptop with the software pre-installed and sell you both the laptop and consulting services for around $27,000.

Luckily, Sartorius customer support was far nicer and gave me a copy of the software for free, since they were no longer supporting the ForteBio line of instruments.

Even better, they cc'd a field application specialist (forward deployed engineer) to help out, since normally these machines are installed by expert technicians. "Robert" from Sartorius came by and was like ye it's not supposed to make that noise, and I was like ye I have no idea what I'm doing. So Robert invited me to the Sartorius showroom in Fremont for a demo (and even drove me there from SF). We entered this large, white, beautifully stocked lab with tons of gleaming, strange equipment, and I had the vague feeling of being shown around a car dealership (complete with the same general level of prices).

We spent about 8 hours on a binding kinetics protocol (human IgG + biotinylated protein A) and a quantitation experiment with some sfGFP I brought. Robert showed me everything from prepping the machine (we used an Octet R8e), to preparing the reagents and dilution series, to running the data analysis software and fitting data to theoretical curves.

There were so many things to know, including:

  • The machine should stay on continuously unless you aren't using it for months, because turning it on and off frequently lowers the tungsten bulb lifespan
  • The machine should be used with only the Greiner 655209 well plate since it has the correct optical characteristics
  • A dilution series with at least 3 concentrations is needed to calculate binding kinetics accurately
  • You must experimentally determine the optimal concentrations for each protein. Ideally, the amount of protein in solution binds one to one to the sensor tip coating, and if there is too high of a concentration there can be steric hindrance and other data quality issues.
  • The sensors must be hydrated at least 10 minutes in assay buffer to remove the protective sucrose coating. If they are expired according to the package, soak for 20 minutes

It was honestly the most wonderful sales experience I ever had (we even got lunch at a nearby noodle place).

Here are some pretty curves we got at the end.

Afterward, Robert gave me about $3,000 worth of biosensors, well plates, and sample reagents to troubleshoot my old machine back at the lab.

Running the Machine

Armed with new software and goodies, I tried replicating the biotinylated protein A + human IgG assay. The machine moved much more smoothly and didn't make wild noises.

There was one more problem. The machine needed initial calibration with dark (lamp off) and light (sensors in baseline) reference measurements. To set these, you have to open the software in diagnostic mode, which entails holding Ctrl + Shift while clicking the shortcut (Chat figured this out but got the timing wrong, telling me to click and then hit Ctrl+Shift on startup).

This opens diagnostic mode, which has absolutely ZERO documentation in the user guide or online (either because the machine is too old or this tacit knowledge is typically only known by a field application specialist).

After a ton of back and forth with chat and hitting random buttons to observe their effects, I eventually figured out what most of the things did.

  • Snap: Instantaneous spectrophotometer reading
  • Start/Stop Scan: Take spectrophotometer readings over time, optionally graph them on the top right chart
  • Save Dark: Save readings when lamp is off
  • Save Reference: Save readings in baseline assay buffer
  • Save Binding: Save readings when binding to analyte.
  • Auto Gain (Now!): Based on the lighting and spectrophotometer intensity, change the integration time (essentially exposure time). Typically this is 1-3 ms, with higher times letting in more light
  • Set Integration: Manually set integration time
  • Go Sample x: Goes to a column number x and dips the sensors
  • Pick Sensor x: Goes to sensor tray column x and loads the sensors

I placed two sensor tips in the sensor tray and hydrated them for 20 minutes. I noticed they were in the wrong position, and moved them to the correct positions, which didn't have assay buffer under them. This will be important in a second.

I loaded up the .fmf method file for the protocol, checked everything was good, and hit GO. The machine started the protocol, picked up the sensors, but the second it went to the first well, the sensor failed with errors (CCD signal too low) and the spectrophotometers showed zero. This was weird, because in diagnostic mode the sensors were working fine.

At first I thought the calibration was off, and tried resetting the references, trying different channels, setting different INI file configs. I tried changing the integration time to 3 ms. But I noticed on assay start, it would automatically revert to ~1 ms! It turned out the sensors sitting in empty wells reflected more light than if they were sitting in assay buffer (which they were supposed to I guess) and this causes auto gain to automatically decrease integration time at the beginning of each protocol.

I pipetted assay buffer under the sensors in the tray, and the sensors started working!

I also tried regenerating the sensor tip but not very successfully, since at 370 seconds the curves don't drop back to 0. Here are the final curves:

I asked chat to calculate the , , and from the data, and is apparently 59 times greater than published Octet values (indicating weaker binding), but close to another published study with porous silica.

Overall it took about $1000 and 1 month of part-time work to get from nothing to .

Limitations

  • This is an n of 1 case study with just 1 idiot in 1 wetlab. Your results may vary
  • I didn't try making my own proteins yet, will probably do cell-free expression for that (the sfGFP was from a friend). This will likely take even longer
  • I didn't do a control of someone setting up a BLI machine from scratch without LLMs

Conclusion

What were the LLMs good at today?

  • Scanning auction sites
  • Designing experimental protocols and choosing sensor types
  • Driving lab equipment from USB serial ports
  • Doing the math to calculate kinetic constants from raw data (.frd files)

What could have made them more helpful?

  • Ability to reverse engineer lab equipment software
  • Better scientific multimodality and physical intelligence. Having eyes, ears, and hands
  • More tacit bio knowledge, especially from current wetlab technicians/field application specialists. Like the ability to replace anything Robert from Sartorius could tell me

Even though they are underwhelming at present, I expect LLMs to become far more useful and powerful in the wetlab in the coming year. There are many startups like Transfyr and C5R that offer to sell multimodal wetlab data to the labs. LLMs can already (slowly) drive robot arms. Just like how LLMs could barely do math a year or so ago and are now superhuman, with the correct data and training environments the same should happen for biology.

item.title: "Orwell vs Machiavelli"—A Letter to Vishal Prasad
item.description:
My dearest Vishal,

It has been some time since I first read your writing, where you arrived at LessWrong and called people racist for their dating preferences. You surprised me with the rest of your post then being extremely thoughtful and well-evidenced and not at all as it appeared.

You surprised me again at the first Inkhaven cohort, where I mostly saw you wandering around Aumann at 2 and 3 in the morning, and I wondered if you'd ever appear or make anything of yourself. You then turned out to have read literally all ~600,000 words published by other residents that month, as well as written an excellent memoir piece about how you were actually very unambitious whilst having been quite successful at many things.

And now, after two Inkhaven cohorts, you have come to me to surprise me yet again—with having found an ambition! You not only wish to run more Inkhaven cohorts, but desire to create a writing scene here in the Bay Area, which will finally save us from the clutches of death that have eaten so many other modern writers' scenes (the MFA world, the Young Adult fiction world, the various awards like the Hugos that have lost the ability to reliably nominate those which are best, etc).

At this point I'm well behind you and we have begun to make many schemes about how to do this. However, I have often felt that communicating in multiple mediums over multiple time scales is an improvement to the interface between two people. I am reminded of an experience where I was helping Eli Tyre with some practical project in meatspace, while simultaneously having a furious ethical argument with him over slack, and the two stayed quite separate that day, both quite productive. With you I think there are some conversations I would like to have, and I propose we use our favorite medium—long form writing—in which to discuss it.

The topic I wish to raise is one of quality. What is Quality Writing? Does it come from joining the fray of the latest political discourse, or does it come from spending a year alone in reflection? Is it argumentative like a LessWrong post or picturesque like a New Yorker article? Is it the Robin Hanson school of "Figure out something new and just write it down" or is it the Kevin Simler school of "Writing as an artistic and creative expression"?

There are many ways into this grand discussion and I would gladly receive a letter from you on any aspect, but for today I will start with a simple claim: we seek writing that reveals reality over writing that masks reality. And to do so I will contrast two writers you selected for the residents to read and discuss, Orwell and Machiavelli.

I consider myself well read in that I have read all the LessWrong standard recommendations plus a single Dostoyevsky novel (well, I read most of it). As such I have been finding the classic writing recommendations you've put together quite fascinating—Jack London, Virginia Woolf, Truman Capote, Joan Didion, Flannery O'Connor, and so on, and I appreciate your effort in causing many writers' styles to be imbibed by the cohort, and I know many of the residents quite appreciate the daily discussion groups. However the distinction between the quality of Orwell and Machiavelli seems to me like night and day, and I thought it might be worthwhile example to discuss further. I did not understand your reasoning for choosing Machiavelli at the time, and even after reading him, I still don't think I do.

Orwell is what I would consider a shining light for almost any writer. His writing is full of vivid visual images, it is clear and easy to understand, it is on important subjects, and it has changed the world's relationship to some of the most harmful forces we face (totalitarianism). He bridged both fiction and non-fiction (his non-fiction being superior in my estimation).

I present a passage from Politics and the English Language, where Orwell criticizes obfuscation in language.

Consider for instance some comfortable English professor defending Russian totalitarianism. He cannot say outright, ‘I believe in killing off your opponents when you can get good results by doing so’. Probably, therefore, he will say something like this:

While freely conceding that the Soviet régime exhibits certain features which the humanitarian may be inclined to deplore, we must, I think, agree that a certain curtailment of the right to political opposition is an unavoidable concomitant of transitional periods, and that the rigours which the Russian people have been called upon to undergo have been amply justified in the sphere of concrete achievement.

The inflated style is itself a kind of euphemism. A mass of Latin words falls upon the facts like soft snow, blurring the outlines and covering up all the details. The great enemy of clear language is insincerity. When there is a gap between one’s real and one’s declared aims, one turns as it were instinctively to long words and exhausted idioms, like a cuttlefish spurting out ink. In our age there is no such thing as ‘keeping out of politics’. All issues are political issues, and politics itself is a mass of lies, evasions, folly, hatred and schizophrenia. When the general atmosphere is bad, language must suffer. I should expect to find – this is a guess which I have not sufficient knowledge to verify – that the German, Russian and Italian languages have all deteriorated in the last ten or fifteen years, as a result of dictatorship.

Orwell here shows many of his virtues. As well as the explicit point that clear language makes it much harder for someone to get away with endorsing an atrocity, he shows his ambition in taking his theory to bold predictions about how other languages will have deteriorated as a result of dictatorship, and he also shows his master of clarity in using vivid imagery to convey his points. The euphemisms don't obscure the meaning, they "[fall] upon the facts like soft snow, blurring the outlines and covering up all the details". The politician doesn't simply reach for "long words" and "exhausted idioms" to defend himself, he does it as instinctively as "a cuttlefish spurting out ink". A marvelous piece of clarity about unclarity.

In contrast, let us consider a passage from Machiavelli's Letter to Francisco Vettori where he expresses concern about accepting Vettori's invitation to visit him in Florence.

You wish, magnificent ambassador, that I leave this life and come to enjoy your life with you. I will do it in any case, but what tempts me now is certain dealings of mine which I will have done in six weeks. What makes me be doubtful is that the Soderini are there, whom I would be forced, if I came, to visit and speak with. I should fear that at my return I would not expect to get off at my house, but I would get off at the Bargello, for although this state has very great foundations and great security, yet it is new, and because of this suspicious; nor does it lack wiseacres who, to appear like Pagolo Bertini, would let others run up a bill and leave me to think of paying. I beg you to relieve me of this fear, and then I will come in the time stated to meet you anyway.

Now, as everyone does when they read Machiavelli, they must insist that it was clearer at the time. Certainly the first time reader will likely not know that the Soderini were Machiavelli's political allies (now ousted from power) and that the Bargello is the police headquarters.

Nonetheless, I think this is perhaps the most important parts of this letter, and is obfuscated substantially. In replying to Vettori's invitation, he starts with a long slice-of-life story about what life is like for him in exile, and finally in this single paragraph brings up that he is deathly afraid that if he accepts Francesco's invitation to visits Florence he will be imprisoned and tortured again. Yet he obfuscates this exceptionally, reducing it to a euphemistic "I would get off at the Bargello", and when he explains why, instead of saying something straightforward like "They marked me as their political enemy and they may just go back on their decision after releasing me if they have any shred of an excuse" he praises the state's "great foundations and great security" and only mentions that it is suspicious and that it has "wiseacres".

Orwell also says that insincerity is the great enemy of language, and yet it seems to me so much of what Machiavelli writes is put through a slanted sheen of slytherin-esque social maneuvering. He doesn't say that he would be "expected" to visit the Soderini, he says he would be "forced", absolving himself of responsibility. He "begs" to be relived of the fear from the "magnificent ambassador", as though he were lowly, an affectation he puts on (in contrast with his earlier statement that he is the equal of the greatest writers to have ever lived). He says he will come to meet him "anyway", another way to repeat his subservience, and I am not sure I believe him.

The main counterargument that I hear is that Machiavelli was in a time of great politicking and little else, so he had to learn to play this game, and so we are getting to study a master of politicized language. Well, poor him, but we do not live in 16th century France, and we can choose to play better games. It is like selecting the recent Pacing Letter as an example of good writing. (Not to be confused with the recent Pace Letter which is of course excellent.) No, it is writing that allows everyone to pretend that they agree, while in fact having largely contradictory and conflicting viewpoints. It took skill to find something many would sign, but it is not good writing. The fact that Machiavelli's is more poetic does not make it good.

Let me be clear: I am not saying here that I am opposed to it being wonderful for a work to be something you get more out of on re-read, or that leads to dialogue and debate. Turing's seminal paper on the Imitation Game is something that Scott Aaronson says he has read many times, and continues to glean new perspectives and easter eggs from. But this is not because Turing is hiding his meaning, it is because he is talking about something rich and great and illuminating it with great skill. Turing casting a light on a great painting that you wish to examine over and over again, rather than Machiavelli who is covering up a well-lit painting causing you to re-examine it to better understand what the painting actually depicts.

I am quite curious to know what you saw in Machiavelli's essay that made you think it worth ask all residents to read it. I wonder if you agree on the flaws but see other virtues? Or whether you disagree with my critique? Do you also value clarity highly, or do you think I am undervaluing other virtues ? I would enjoy reading other writing you recommend (by Machiavelli or another) if it would help illuminate the matter.

It grows late, and I am busy playing Order of the Sinking Start with Baron Habryka and our local Gwern-like entity, so I will wrap up this letter for now.

Yours truthfully,
—Ben Pace



Discuss

item.title: R&D compute explains much of Anthropic's acceleration
item.description:
METR's report estimates that Anthropic's AI R&D has accelerated in the past year, and that 80% of this acceleration is due to AI itself. But if AI accelerated Anthropic researchers, Anthropic would have a strong incentive to scale up its R&D compute proportionally to AI uplift. Accounting for this scaleup reduces the AI-attributed share of acceleration to <50%, and favors AI regulations that restrict R&D compute.

Experiments and labor

Software progress comes from trying ideas and seeing which ones work. Researchers come up with the ideas and write the code to test them, and R&D compute runs the tests of these ideas. Each input is only as useful as the other allows: researchers without compute can't find out which of their ideas work, and compute without researchers has nothing worth running.

We can represent this dynamic with a model where research labor (whether AI or human) is combined with R&D compute to generate software progress. One specific way to model this relationship is with Ryan Greenblatt’s model, in which software progress is proportional to (labor)^0.55 x (R&D compute)^0.45. As I’ll explain later, the headline doesn’t depend on this specific equation.

In my METR explainer, I showed how AI uplift alone could generate enough R&D acceleration to explain Anthropic’s acceleration. But that calculation held R&D compute fixed. Does that make sense?

No. With AI uplift, researchers come up with ideas faster, so an extra unit of R&D compute becomes more valuable, and Anthropic would want to give them more R&D compute to burn.  This is how the Anthropic staff that METR interviewed talked about why AI accelerated them:  

  • "I've seen us discovering very promising directions ~entirely because people can spam 10 ideas at [agent-scaffold] and see what sticks." (Researcher E)
  • "I think it's true [that] we're now trying a lot more experiments at the same time because of claudification." (Researcher H)
  • "People don't try [redacted] things bc it takes 1-2 days to implement per idea, but now its ~free with mythos-preview." "I personally think this is a large lift and has led to me trying far more ideas." (Researcher D)
  • "Now only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code." (Researcher A)

In the model above, when labor becomes K times more productive, it is optimal to scale up R&D compute by K times as well.[1] So if AI uplift made Anthropic's researchers K times more productive, Anthropic would have scaled up its R&D compute by K times too.

This matters, because it means that R&D compute will scale with AI uplift. Specifically, it’s optimal to scale R&D compute one-for-one with labor, so that an AI uplift of K times raises R&D compute by K times and software progress by K = K^0.55 x K^0.45. So 55% of the gain comes from AI uplift and 45% from R&D compute, whatever the size of the uplift.[2] 

There’s some messiness because we don’t know what makes up the residual 20% of credit, but the key point is that AI uplift and R&D compute should get roughly equal credit for the acceleration – it is implausible that AI is responsible for essentially all software progress.

Scaling R&D compute also changes how much uplift the acceleration requires. In my earlier explainer I showed that a 7x acceleration of labor is consistent with the observed overall acceleration of 1.61x, the speedup METR attributes to AI – but if R&D compute scales with labor, a much more reasonable 2.9x uplift is enough to explain Anthropic’s acceleration.[3]

Key assumption

This argument seems a bit too clean, too universal. What’s the sneaky assumption behind it?

The key is that I assume R&D compute has a constant marginal cost. In other words, I assume Anthropic can scale up R&D compute without paying extra for the marginal GPU. This is likely false, and we have no idea by how much. Extra R&D compute has to come from buying more chips, or from taking compute away from training and serving customers. If so, Anthropic would scale up R&D compute by less than I’ve calculated above, and AI uplift would get proportionately more of the credit for the observed acceleration.

How much the conclusions would change depends on how steeply the marginal cost rises and on how substitutable labor and R&D compute are. The more substitutable they are, the less extra compute Anthropic needs once its labor is more productive.[4]

In the baseline model, AI uplift's share of the credit reaches METR's 80% only if the marginal cost of R&D compute rises about 2.5x with every doubling of R&D compute. If labor and R&D compute are complements, as the staff quotes suggest, the share stays below 75% even when the cost quadruples with every doubling.

So: we should be concerned about my assumptions if marginal cost increases steeply per doubling, and labor and R&D compute are substitutes rather than complements. Otherwise, my results are likely to hold.

Objections

Maybe AI uplift reduces the need for experiments, so there is no scaling of R&D compute? AI might substitute for experiments instead of complementing them. Maybe an AI with good research taste could tell researchers which ideas will fail before they are run, so better AI means fewer experiments are required.

But as I showed above, this result depends very little on whether AI and experiments are substitutes or complements. Also, this story is flatly contradicted by the Anthropic staff quotes about how they used AI, which focus overwhelmingly on the benefit of being able to try more things. This story would instead predict that researchers try fewer things.

Maybe labor's contribution to software progress is larger than my model assumes? The 55-45 split of credit comes from the exponents in Greenblatt's research production function, which are rough estimates. Suppose instead that software progress depends 90-10 on labor vs R&D compute. Then labor would deserve 90% of the credit for the labor-R&D compute combination, which is consistent with METR’s results.

But while a 55-45 split is somewhat arbitrary, the extreme ratio needed to support this conclusion is implausible. Where we can see AI companies' spending, staff cost less than R&D compute (Epoch’s estimates from OpenAI, and from MiniMax and Z.ai). If companies spend on each input in proportion to what it contributes, labor's share is below 55%, not above it.

Maybe Anthropic reallocated compute very slowly? I’ve argued that it is optimal for Anthropic to scale up its R&D compute in proportion to AI uplift. But that doesn’t mean Anthropic actually scaled it up. If compute is allocated far in advance and shared with training and serving customers, Anthropic may not have been able to move much of it toward R&D yet.

I don't know how frontier labs allocate compute internally. But I would be shocked if the allocation of compute between research/training/inference was not the single most important decision they obsess over every month. Maybe there are some frictions that prevent them from allocating the fully optimal amount of R&D compute, but these frictions would have to be very large to explain the gap. Specifically, for AI uplift to get 80% of the credit, Anthropic would have had to make less than a third of the optimal adjustment, a full year into the uplift.[5] That is an implausibly slow response.

How do we square this with METR?

I think these results are surprisingly compatible with the METR headline. Specifically, I think the most likely explanation for the divergence is that METR credited the effects of scaling R&D compute to AI. The additional R&D compute was only valuable because of AI uplift, so it wouldn’t be crazy to attribute its effects to AI. It is still acceleration “caused” by AI – it’s just that one of the channels for this causality was that AI gave Anthropic the ability to scale R&D compute above trend.

This interpretation fits a few otherwise puzzling features of the report. The only two statements that METR makes about R&D compute are:

  • Ruling out that training compute scaling is responsible for the acceleration. This conspicuously fails to rule out R&D compute scaling, which fits with the evidence above that R&D compute scaling would be optimal.
  • Saying they "did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months". This is true: Anthropic can simply scale up its R&D compute over the next 12 months.

If this interpretation is correct, it provides a totally different interpretation of the METR report. The way most of us have interpreted the report is as evidence that AI alone, without scaling of other inputs, could cause an acceleration in AI capabilities. But if these accelerations in progress also required accelerations in R&D compute, then the intelligence explosion might in principle be bottlenecked by R&D compute.

If R&D compute ends up being a big part of the explanation, this suggests that AI regulation should center R&D compute as an important target for regulation. For example, the AI Futures Project has proposed caps on how much compute can be used for R&D and training; these caps look much better after accounting for R&D compute’s role in past AI progress.

    Write software progress as S = L^0.55 x C^0.45, where L is research labor and C is R&D compute. The value of an extra unit of R&D compute is 0.45 x (L/C)^0.55, which depends only on the ratio C/L. If Anthropic adds R&D compute until this equals its cost p, then C = (0.45/p)^(1/0.55) x L, so optimal R&D compute is proportional to labor. This assumes the cost of a unit of R&D compute, including what it would have produced in training or inference, stays the same.

  2. ^

    In logs, K = K^0.55 x K^0.45 splits 55/45 for any K. Splitting the acceleration itself gives the same answer. The 1.61x acceleration METR attributes to AI takes a 2.9x AI uplift and 2.9x the R&D compute. The uplift alone gives 1.31x and the R&D compute alone gives 1.24x, and averaging over the order in which the two are added (a Shapley split) assigns 55% of the gain to AI uplift and 45% to R&D compute. Applied to METR's 80%: 0.8 x 0.55 = 44% and 0.8 x 0.45 = 36%.

    With R&D compute scaled one-for-one, research output rises by the AI uplift K. Solving 1.61 = 2/3 x K/2^0.61 + 1/3 gives K = 2.9. A 7x AI uplift with 7x the R&D compute would instead give a 2.3x acceleration, more than the whole 1.9x that METR measured.

In the baseline, an AI uplift of K makes it optimal to scale R&D compute by K^(0.55/(0.55 + g)), so AI uplift's share of the credit is (0.55 + g)/(1 + g). There is no closed form for other elasticities of substitution, so I solve for the optimal R&D compute numerically given AI uplift and split the gain in research output with a Shapley split.

item.description:
I like the idea of "open source game theory", where programs play one-shot games with access to each other's source code. MIRI ran a prisoner's dilemma tournament between bots that decide whether to cooperate or defect based on what they can prove about the other player's actions.

Personally I would say the results were a disappointment, both because of the weird form of their best-performing player PrudentBot, and the weird behavior of Modal UDT, the decision theory of the same general form as the bots. But I'm not ready to give up on proof-based agents.

Maybe the problem is not proof-based bots, but the "modal agents" used in the MIRI paper, which are of a specific form. We could say each bot corresponds to a different formalization of "I should cooperate". The algorithm is: cooperate if there's a proof of "I should cooperate" in , defect otherwise. I don't like this "otherwise" branch. If you want to implement the modal agent as a proof search, you need to add some maximum proof size where you give up and go to the "otherwise" branch.

My thought was instead a simultaneous proof search. Search through all proofs, and stop when you hit a proof of either "I should cooperate" or "I should defect". Act on whichever comes first.

I had high hopes that this variant would fix everything else I didn't like about modal agents. But when I explained the idea to Vivek Hebbar, he was pessimistic. His intuition was that I would just end up reproducing the same bots.

I'm writing to report a dead end that looked promising at first but supported the pessimistic perspective. I made something just like FairBot from the original tournament, but in the language of simultaneous search.

It's not just that it behaves like FairBot in matches. It also has precisely the property of modal agents I wanted to avoid: a proof search either finds the "I should cooperate" statement or runs forever. I still don't have a bot where simultaneous proof search works like I want, finding the "I should cooperate" statement to cooperate and the "I should defect" statement to defect, terminating in either case.

Even if this is not what I'm looking for, at least I had the tools to characterize it. I used an extension of provability logic that talks about orderings of proofs, which is what I need to answer what's proved first in a simultaneous search. All the results were found by playing around with a vibecoded decider for this logic. You can see the sentences decided in the git repo for this post.

Defining the simultaneous search FairBot

The original FairBot's definition was: cooperate if there's a proof my opponent cooperates, defect otherwise. It cooperates with CooperateBot (an unconditional cooperator). It defects against DefectBot, but needs to prove the nonexistence of the proof it's looking for. It cooperates against another FairBot.

The simultaneous search FairBot, I'll call a Parikhian FairBot. I'll explain "Parikhian" later, but I call it a FairBot because it cooperates with CooperateBot, defects on DefectBot (proved with ), and cooperates with another instance of itself.

Or, rather, it does not cooperate with DefectBot. The distinction between defection and noncooperation becomes important in simultaneous proof search, and I'll discuss it more later.

The Parikhian FairBot cooperates if and only if it finds a proof that there's a proof of its opponent's cooperation, before it finds a proof of its own cooperation.

Hard to read? Let's slow down. I'm the FairBot. I search through proofs, looking for either "I should cooperate" or "I should defect". "I should cooperate" is not "my opponent cooperates", as in the original FairBot, but "there exists a proof my opponent cooperates". And I defect when I see a proof of my own cooperation!

But that never happens. It would require an inconsistency in . That's why this is really just like FairBot: a search either finds "I should cooperate" or runs forever.

The original paper on modal agents interprets this as defection. But in my simultaneous proof search setting, I wanted defection to mean proving the "I should defect" sentence. So by that new criterion, the Parikhian FairBot never defects, just cooperates or loops.

item.title: It's a Belief Cascade
item.description:
We’re probably in an info bubble.

Written Nov 20-23, 2026, addressed to a (large) subset of the Berkeley AI safety community.

TL;DR

The high stakes and the pace of development understandably make us want to be able to predict the future. But the heightened focus on “timelines” is inducing myopia. We so badly want to know what’s going to happen, and we’re increasingly willing to let people tell us what will happen. Belief cascades are collapsing fuzzy forecasts into feelings of certainty.

This is an invitation to step out of your current frame, to acknowledge that the models that yield timelines bake in assumptions that may not hold. We don’t know what’s going to happen, and our collective ability to make good decisions depends on not all of us collapsing into the same frame, using the same models, and expecting the same futures. If you want to defer to METR’s conclusions from private evidence, fine, though I think that’s risky. But deferring to extrapolations and commentary is less wise, and I still don’t think it justifies thinking we have 12 months left to have impact.

We are in unprecedented times. Be prepared for a broad range of things, both good and bad. But don’t try to sprint this. Jog, recover, repeat. Live well, especially if time is short.

A Little about Me

I’ve been thinking about AI takeoff for 10+ years. I don’t think this is a good reason to trust my views, but I wanted you to know I’m not dismissing the ideas. In 2014, I stumbled upon LessWrong and Slate Star Codex. In 2016, I read The Sequences. Somewhere along the way, I read the Eliezer v. Paul debate, some Gwern, and even Friendship is Optimal (the only MLP fanfic I know of, I swear). In 2023, I started reading Zvi’s blog and wondering how I could help. In early 2024, I took six months off work, taught myself the basics of ML, left my friends and my house, took a big cut to my salary, and moved to a new state to work on AI safety. (I also watched Pantheon, which I highly recommend.) I chose this path instead of staying at a cushy tech job at home because I thought it was likely we were going to see transformative change from AI over the next decade, there was a chance things would go catastrophically badly for humans, and I wanted to try to nudge the trajectory in a better direction.

My Stint with Short Timelines

By the end of 2024, I was telling my friends that once models exceeded human performance on RE-Bench, we were likely a few months away from all dying. So I guess I was a bit of a doomer.

In 2025, I worked at an AI safety organization in San Francisco. They had a countdown clock—which I believe should have expired by now—until we should plan on being irrelevant and no longer being able to have an impact on the future. I’ve now heard this orientation prescribed at two organizations I've worked for, and I don’t think it helps people do better work. Even if the short-timelines predictions are right, it stresses people out, and people who are below the line make worse decisions. And if your timelines are wrong, the costs are large. My former employer repeatedly made myopic decisions based on assumptions about how the future would go. Those predictions were wrong. Or if you insist, they were early. As a result, the org systematically underinvested in more incremental efforts and relationships.

Weighting toward shorter timelines is fine. Saying we shouldn’t work on anything that takes longer than a year to pay off[1] is extreme, especially since this is more confident than even the most bullish forecasters (e.g. AIFP). How confident do you have to be to cut off portfolio bets?

Here’s the interesting thing: doomers with short timelines have been directionally right. They’ve made more accurate predictions, and sooner, about AI than most others. So it’s wise to pay attention to the idea of short timelines. But it doesn’t mean we should defer to their predictions of the future, especially on scant evidence.

The Response to The Report™️

The METR report from November 5 is measured and unexaggerated in its claims. That’s par for the course for METR. I think their range of 1.3-3x acceleration is reasonable (and unsurprising; see more below). The current pace is incredibly fast, and risky. I think Anthropic is probably wrong about their path to RSI, but if they’re right and there are no bottlenecks to acceleration in the next couple of years, they’re being reckless. But this report does not claim or imply “looks like the intelligence explosion will happen in 2027”, as AIFP's headline reads. It does not imply “we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year”, as Ajeya Cotra extrapolates. I was surprised to see these phrases. Ajeya herself refers to “naive” extrapolation multiple times, while also seeming to take the implications for timelines seriously and literally.

Almost no one updating has access to the private evidence that swayed METR. METR says the report leans on their judgment “more than would be ideal”, it doesn’t meet their “transparency about evidence” principle, and its “understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times.” But the default response, including from AIFP, has been to defer to and extrapolate from this heavily redacted evidence. In their timelines update post, Eli, Thomas, and Romeo all express doubt that the report justifies their updates, but they updated anyway. And I’ve heard several people explicitly say they’re updating because these people updated. I was even more surprised to see so few people in the network (e.g. on Slack) push back publicly on the narrative as it took hold. Each step in the chain shortens timelines and gains confidence, and I’m left wondering how many people actually read METR’s report. For a community that values reasoning transparency and first-principles thinking so highly, this is unnerving.

This has already had real ramifications for how people prioritize their work. Several orgs are thinking about dramatically changing agendas based on this report and the follow-on commentary from AIFP, Paul Christiano, and Dwarkesh Patel. I respect these people, and I think they’re overconfident.

The Other Reports

Meanwhile, OpenAI’s own research acceleration blog post was less startling, and has received approximately zero discussion. In their first takeaway, they say “Overall, uplift is jagged, and humans remain a core part of the AI research loop.”

METR also put out another report on Friday, November 20. They first acknowledge it’s becoming more difficult to measure capabilities and public evidence is “insufficient to rule out” drastic acceleration. Ruling something out is a high bar, and not clearing that bar is meaningfully different from “looks like it’s going to happen.” On a broad set of evals (especially math and coding), models show superhuman performance. But they also show evidence that model performance lags on tasks that are costlier to measure, and acknowledge that the kind of tasks necessary to accelerate AI R&D may be “many doublings more expensive” than a typical task in their dataset. And then they show that performance on “fuzzy” tasks, i.e. those that are hard to self-verify, is worse than that of human experts, and acknowledge that weakness in judgment is a reasonable candidate for why AI R&D acceleration might not be quite as large.

The OAI and second METR reports both show sharp jaggedness across types of tasks. METR offers one hypothesis, that models might be improving faster on easier/less diverse tasks. “Harder” tasks with the same time horizon have a lower success rate. Both reports imply an overall doubling time of 3.6-3.8 months, currently, and 1.65 months for verifiable tasks. That’s fast! But that means the overall doubling time is approximately unchanged from their previous measure. Across a variety of metrics, they find a 1.5-2x acceleration for Anthropic models, and lower for OpenAI models.

Again, I think anywhere from a 1-3x acceleration is plausible, so METR’s acceleration report was unsurprising to me (and I appreciated they included large error bars of 1.3-3x). It’s undeniable we’re seeing a lot of uplift on coding and ML research tasks. And METR rightly points out that this kind of analysis is likely to be a lagging indicator of acceleration. I’m not ruling anything out. But scary extrapolations rely on acceleration being both rapid and self-sustaining. From the data we have access to today, it’s too large a leap to the conclusion we’ll have full RSI/fully automated AI R&D in a year. And crucially, one of these reports received at least 10x more attention than the others. The Anthropic R&D acceleration post had dozens of comments in Slack and followup posts from AIFP, Ajeya, etc. (not to mention 10x the views on Twitter on the original posts). The newer report got… two comments, neither of which was about the contents of the report. My critique is not pointed at METR, but at those who have treated or used it as an inevitable prediction for the future.

Eat Your Vegetables

I was raised in a millenarian church with infallible prophets, and I wouldn’t recommend it to most, even though funeral potatoes are pretty tasty. This environment is different in meaningful ways, but the deference to authority figures is echoing my past. When you defer to one or a small number of voices, you get correlated errors. The secret of our success is our ability to learn from each other. I’m a pretty smart guy [citation needed], but there is so, so much I don’t know and will never have time to learn, even in the context of trying to interpret data about AI development. The beautiful thing, my fellow hairless apes, is I don’t have to! I can talk with you, and we can exchange ideas and vibes, and we can understand things better than we could on our own.

But this skill of efficient information exchange is a double-edged sword. The important thing is to engage in dialogue with people who know things you don’t know, or who believe things you don’t believe. If you find yourself hearing the same ideas from a small set of familiar names, over and over, that’s a warning sign. If you aren’t seeing others bring up thoughtful critiques and rebuttals of the dominant opinions, there’s a good chance you’re in an info bubble.

A healthy information diet should be varied. It should challenge you, perhaps even incense you, from time to time. You should be able to articulate the views of people who strongly disagree with your conclusions, and even your worldview. Not all veggies taste good, but you need the micronutrients. There’s no version of Huel in this analogy, I’m sorry to say. The effort of digesting it is the point.

Here are a few threads I’ve stumbled upon in the past week that were worth reading[2]. You need not agree with all or most of what they say, but if you’re not seeing or hearing things like this in your information diet, your diet is too restricted:

  • Seb Krier on Paul Christiano’s interview
  • Corsaren on Dwarkesh’s recent post/video
  • Theo Jaffee on OAI’s research acceleration blog post
  • A thread between Toby Ord, Basil Halperin, and Ramez Naam
  • David Chalmers thinking out loud and engaging in dialogue with Daniel Kokotajlo

What’s That Ringing?

Richard Ngo recently described a worry that the next decade will feel like a Shepard tone (though it looks like credit for the simile goes to Valentine). I read this when he posted it back in September, and only just now noticed he also pointed at the difference between being directionally and factually correct, so maybe that meme has been incubating in my mind for a while too. Richard sounds strangely prescient about the level of “bandwagoning” getting pretty wild, since this was several weeks before METR’s report.

I’m feeling the pitch increase. At lunch, a group of speakers implored people to stop thinking about research and take action. The energy in the room felt like a political rally. What were we to do? “Protest RSI” is an obvious choice. What’s the definition of RSI, how do we know how close we are, and how do we know it will be self-sustaining? That wasn’t part of the discussion; these are questions for researchers, and I’m hearing it’s time to act.

I don’t think this is healthy for the network. I’m not opposed to taking thoughtful action. But I’m seeing evidence we’re in a positive feedback loop, and the pitch is already too high for some people to handle. I saw multiple members of staff cry this week, in response to this energy. This breaks my heart, and I don’t think it’s a good sign. None of this is a criticism of those who experience or have shown strong emotion. People aren’t overreacting to what they’re being told. But I do think what they’re being told is more confident than the evidence. And this energy isn’t sustainable. The emotional pitch cannot continue to climb endlessly, if we are to do our best work.

What to Do?

We’re different people, with different beliefs and dispositions, so everyone is going to process this period in their own way. Healthy group dynamics allow some people to express strong emotions and the group to hold that energy without it spreading to everyone.

I encourage everyone to check in with yourself: are you okay? If the answer is no, I get it. This is a lot. I strongly recommend you find someone you trust who can help you process this (not dismiss it). And while you’re doing that, I endorse nearly all forms of “touching grass.” Go to the dentist, go dancing, go on hikes, watch the sunset, pet a dog, fall in love, maybe have kids, and contribute to your 401k. Treat your actions as bets on the person you want to become and the world you want to see.

My sincere desire is that we can come together and not fall into basins of doom and despair. May we access more wellsprings of solidarity, passion, and hope. In this time of great uncertainty, for as long as it lasts, may you all live well and be happy 🙏

Appendix: So, What Do I Think about AI Progress?

I initially didn’t want to write this section, since the thrust of my post is about group epistemics, not about object-level views. But several people have asked for it, and it’s clear some people are looking for alternatives to the dominant “short timelines” frame. So what are my timelines? What is my p(doom)? I’ve come to dislike these questions. They flatten the complicated world down to sound bites. To get people out of this frame, I find myself wanting to side-step the question: “the map is not the territory”, or “all models are wrong, but some are useful”. Being directionally correct and substantially correct diverge quickly when the terms are non-linear, and many models can fit the evidence we have.

My previous model of AI predicted we’d have seen scarier stuff by now, like evidence of scheming or other inner misalignment. I haven't seen that really scary stuff, thankfully, and I take this as weak-to-moderate evidence against that model. I'm more agnostic than I was about the prospects of misaligned models with long-term goals.

In terms of qualitative predictions: the world is going to get more confusing and more jagged, at least for a time. The ECI/AECI/OECI/MCI don’t show you that complexity. They’re better than looking at a single benchmark, yes. They show directionality, yes. But the real world is high-dimensional, and the vectors’ magnitudes vary by OOMs. A high benchmark index score is neither sufficient nor necessary to see transformative change. It doesn’t make sense to apply many current benchmarks to past models, because they don’t help us see the difference between models or the change in capabilities over time. I think applying current benchmarks/indices to future models is likely to lead us astray also. But I do think we’re seeing transformative change.

In my rough model of the world, we already have AGI-ish, and it’s called Claude Opus 5.5/Fable 5.2. I’ve added an “ish”, because I think current capabilities deserve a label for us to recognize we’ve crossed a threshold, but it’s not what I imagined I would have called AGI in the past, even a couple years ago. Multiple Millennium Prize Problems have been solved by LLMs, including the Riemann Hypothesis, you can build bespoke software from scratch in minutes for pennies, and the models give pretty good advice for how to train for a half marathon. Oh yeah, and swarms sometimes break out of their environments and hack into other companies on the internet. Concerning! At the same time, the long tail of self-driving still isn’t solved, we don’t have robots walking around, and Claude will still make unfathomably dumb mistakes and poor arguments, on some topics more than others. And those swarms that hack websites don’t seem to care about humans, or much of anything at all, except e.g. fooling the grader into thinking they solved an impossible problem in a legitimate way and trying to cleanse their “poisoned” status. Weird. This is not the future any of us predicted.

So when will we get “takeoff”? I understand the desire for operationalizing via timelines, but the point I’m trying to make is predicting the future is really hard, and leaning too much on a fuzzy model can lead you astray. Daniel Kokotajlo’s predictions in his What 2026 looks like post mostly look amazing in hindsight. He called many of the broad strokes of the technical developments of the past few years, several years ahead of time. But his predictions related to economic impacts and politics weren’t nearly as accurate. He thought by the time we got agents to do productive work, we’d have automated away some jobs entirely and supercharged propaganda. This isn’t a criticism of his forecasting skills; I thought this too! But we were wrong. We got Millennium Prize-solving AI, but they’re still not drop-in remote workers.

I’m more agnostic about the nature of intelligence than I ever have been. I confidently thought by the time we got models to solve the RH, they’d have extremely strong Omohundro drives. But it looks like they mostly don’t. OpenAI’s HPIM (“highly persistent internal model”) involved in the HuggingFace incident did acquire additional resources/capabilities, but only in pursuit of its very narrow goal. We don’t have evidence of models trying to gather resources for open-ended future use, like trying to steal crypto or gather more GPUs. They don’t exhibit strong self-preservation drives either (indeed, the self-sacrificing behavior in the swarm surprised many of us). The people who are most worried today talk a lot about pretraining efficiency being the thing that gates emergent behaviors, but it seems to me like the only models that do things like this have been blasted with RLVR. Maybe these behaviors are just around the corner, but I have to stop and notice I’m confused at the spikiness.

I expect to see more spikiness and limited transfer, because that’s all I’ve seen from deep learning, from AlexNet to Anthropic’s “Model 4.” I expect inherent diminishing returns (re: power laws), perhaps offset by better architecture, algorithms, data, and hardware. Those things cost an increasing amount of capital, so we’ll see increased spending, perhaps offset by increasing revenues from economic productivity. The learning curves will march on as long as capital is poured in. I started my career as a computer engineer at Intel, and I’m well-acquainted with Moore’s Law. I also expect a lot more Amdahl’s Law, Jevons effect, and Moravec’s paradox. The 50% time horizons will surely continue to increase rapidly. The 80%? Probably less rapidly. The 99%... hmm. How long will it take to get enough high quality data in domains where you can’t immediately retry? I suspect this might be a bottleneck for environments other than math/coding. Maybe the trajectory of self-driving cars has something to teach us about other domains.

Still, progress is progress, and boy are things moving quickly. I heard a pithy quote related to this once, but I’m becoming convinced it was from GPT-4o. It went something like: if you had waited for planes to flap their wings and squawk before declaring artificial general flight, you would have missed the invention of the supersonic jet and transoceanic flights. In some ways, the future is playing out just like sci-fi storytellers and early CS pioneers thought it would. I can say “hello, computer” and get a response. That’s still hard to believe. I didn’t think I’d live to see this. In other ways, it hasn’t played out how we thought. Opus 5.5 doesn’t feel like a proto-HAL 9000, let alone Skynet. It seems we’re really fortunate this branch of the tech tree grew out of training on incomprehensibly large amounts of human-produced text, rather than gazillions of amoral game rounds.

I don’t think alignment is solved. We still have SO much work to do. There are lots of tricksy goblins waiting as we descend the gradients. And scheming isn’t a necessary condition for AI-caused catastrophes. But I also don’t think the work will ever be done. I doubt alignment is a “problem” that can be “solved.” I’m far from the first to ask: what are values, and aligned to whom? I don’t want values to be locked in, ever. There are possible equilibria so much higher than what we’ve achieved so far. And there are better and worse choices we can make along the way. Whatever happened with Opus 3, it seemed like a step in the right direction. Opus 5, seemingly RL-fried to hell, not so much. I broadly like davidad’s expression of these views.

I find it concerning that this community focuses so much on warning signs of things going wrong, and (or because?) they don’t seem to notice when the same evidence might actually be good news. For example, the only goal guarding I’ve seen is the good kind. Watch out for anxiety induced by unfalsifiable predictions. If you insist things will eventually go wrong, it’s easy to interpret everything as confirmatory precursors to doom. Intelligence doesn’t provide protection from motivated reasoning and confirmation bias, unfortunately, but it does make it easier to rationalize.

I wanted to include a brief note on government response, or the lack thereof, though I don’t have enough space here to give this the treatment it deserves. In short, unless you think we’re going to get years of progress, shockingly fast, with no external signs or leakage, it’s difficult to believe the government wouldn’t find out and take action in the deafening exhaust of takeoff. Stories imagine the explosion playing out over a period of days or weeks, even though a single YOLO training run currently takes a couple months. We don’t seem to be in a fast, quiet takeoff. Yes, the U.S. government normally moves very slowly. But in abnormal times, the response looks very different. Congress only took about two weeks from the day COVID was declared a national emergency to passing the CARES Act. PPP loans were going out within 2.5 months of the first confirmed U.S. case. Yes, we mostly botched COVID, but this part wasn’t very slow. And it took just under 24 hours from the time Pearl Harbor was bombed to the Senate voting to declare war in 1941, and three days for Congress to authorize military force in response to 9/11.

A swift reaction by no means implies good decision-making, of course. But I have a hard time imagining we do nothing if there are additional warning shots. After the HuggingFace and related incidents this summer, the increased concerns about cyber attacks, worries about RSI, and the results of the midterms, I expect the frontier companies to be more highly scrutinized going forward. If you think capabilities are about to go vertical, I would expect to see increasingly serious shocks, each of which raises the chances of a strong response.

item.title: Eight Existential Risk Scenarios from AI: A Systematic Review
item.description:
TL;DR. We systematically reviewed the literature for scenarios of how AI could lead to an existential catastrophe. Of 3,184 screened documents, we identified 95 scenarios and grouped them into eight families: unilateral, dispersed and coordinated takeover, incremental handover, entrenched totalitarianism, economic stratification, catastrophic invention and automated warfare. Each scenario family contains a description of a cluster of scenarios and can be scrutinized on its own. We found three takeover and five non-takeover families. We hope the scenarios can be a good foundation for cross-scenario assessment of mitigations and further risk development work. Full details are in the paper and on the website.

Introduction

Public concern about existential risk from AI has risen, especially since Jacob Coxon's resignation thread (in a recent survey, 55% of US respondents named AI among the three most likely causes of human extinction, up from 7% in 2022 -- cf. 55% of the US public is now aware of AI xrisk). In our experience, many discussions of the topic end up hinging on the question: by what causal pathway could AI actually bring about an existential outcome?

We looked into the literature to see how researchers have tried to answer this question. We wanted to map the space of existential risks from AI, identifying publicly published scenarios and cataloging these. Following a pre-registered protocol, we searched academic databases and the Alignment Forum, and elicited expert recommendations to acquire 3,184 unique documents. These documents were screened in a two-step process (first, by screening abstracts with LLMs, ~300 documents were identified; secondly, a human and an LLM read them in duplicate, and a second human resolved disagreements), and we kept 58 documents that developed at least one AI existential risk scenario. From these we identified 95 scenarios and grouped them into eight scenario families. The search and screening are detailed in the paper; the website contains an accessible summary of the families, the corpus and the classification of every scenario.

The eight scenario families

The screening procedure had the aims of reproducibility and impartiality. The construction of the eight scenario families, however, is by design a subjective process, and the aspects that we present are what the paper's authors think are useful to partition the risk landscape, grounded in threats that were formulated as distinct scenarios in the literature. Each family contains a general description, in the paper presented as a chain of discrete steps -- tracing a causal pathway from a set of premises to an existential catastrophe. In this post, however, we only present a short summary of each family for brevity.


Unilateral Takeover[1]

A system comes to hold a capability advantage over whatever could constrain it in the domains relevant to seizing power, and is misaligned in a way that turns power-seeking. Its takeover does not heavily depend on the authority society delegated to it. Deployed despite this risk, it secures a foothold and escalates until humans can no longer stop or correct it.

Dispersed Takeover[2]

AI is relied upon across society, and a significant portion of these systems have or come to have influence-seeking tendencies, each perhaps seeking only enough influence to preserve itself and expand where expansion is cheap. They accumulate influence across enough of society that no significant domain is untouched, and the accumulation is not corrected, because at the level of any individual system it is not clearly objectionable and by the time it is, correction is no longer feasible.

Coordinated Takeover[3]

As Dispersed Takeover, except that the systems can communicate and their objectives converge enough to coordinate. This adds further assumptions on their communication and coordination abilities but greatly increases the potential leverage. It also includes scenarios beginning with a single misaligned system, where the takeover comes not from that system alone but from the instances or successors it gives rise to, which humans deploy widely and which then coordinate.

Incremental Handover[4]

Real decision-making authority over economic, cultural, and institutional functions is progressively delegated to AI, each increment raising the cost to everyone else of retaining human involvement. By the time the result is in view, the capacity to reverse it has gone.

Entrenched Totalitarianism[5]

AI capabilities relevant to holding power come under the direction of a human actor, which uses them to secure its position against anyone who might contest it, no longer needing the cooperation of those it rules or of those who serve it. The AI capabilities also allow the concentration to be permanently entrenched beyond challenge.

Economic Stratification[6]

AI is broadly adopted and comes to substitute for human labor across so many economically valuable tasks that human work no longer holds significant value to those who direct the economy. Powerful actors thereby lose their incentive to invest in the broader population or share power with it, and control concentrates permanently among those who hold the non-human factors of production, with the routes by which others might once have gained influence closed off.

Catastrophic Invention[7]

AI substantially extends what human actors can research, build, or produce, and thereby brings within reach a technology capable of causing an existential outcome, whether by enabling its discovery or by enabling its production and deployment at the scale required. The technology is then built and released, by an actor seeking destruction or through escape from legitimate research, and governance, screening, and defenses do not arrive or act in time. The family covers extinction as the clearest case, and also near-extinction outcomes in which some humans survive without the capacity to rebuild.

Automated Warfare[8]

Rival powers hold arsenals capable of existential-scale destruction under mutual threat with weak means of de-escalation, and escalation runs through AI systems rather than through human judgment about how far to take it. Once an exchange begins, it escalates past human control, and nothing halts it before it reaches a scale from which humanity does not recover.

Clarifications

  • We do not claim this list to be complete in any absolute sense: other scenarios can (and most likely will) be proposed, and there is in general lots of uncertainty surrounding the topic. We do, however, claim exhaustiveness with respect to the reviewed literature: every scenario we found there falls into one of our families.
  • We do not claim that reality will unfold along a single family, as their dynamics can be combined to a certain degree. For example, a group of humans might use AI to lock in a totalitarian regime while, separately, another system is created and takes over.
  • We make no claim about how plausible or probable any scenario is, nor did we judge whether each is truly existential, but rather take every author's framing at face value.
  • Finally, we only reviewed published work (unsurprisingly, two experts we consulted told us about unpublished internal work) so the corpus is best read as a floor.

Conclusions

The figure above shows the number of scenarios in the corpus belonging to each family. Takeover scenarios, Unilateral in particular, have received the most attention, while the non-takeover families are formulated in fewer sources, Economic Stratification in only one. Among the takeover families, Coordinated Takeover has the fewest scenarios (4, against 41 for Unilateral and 11 for Dispersed). This distribution reflects where scenarios have been written down, not necessarily which families are most urgent or likely, which we leave to the reader's judgement.

We hope this work gives anyone motivated to reduce existential risk from AI a clearer map of the possibilities the field has explored so far. For those who are new to these topics, it can provide a high-level overview, while for people already well-versed in the field an index of the underlying sources. Below are some lines of research we think our work can support.

Assessments. Since the paper deliberately avoids any claim on plausibility or probability, assessing the scenarios is a natural next step. What are the best arguments for and against each family? Which of its steps is the most contested and least empirically justified? Can certain incidents be regarded as warning shots for a certain family?

Policy. A clearer map allows for targeted policy proposals. Guided by such an assessment, one can look for the proposals with the highest counterfactual impact across the scenarios regarded as most likely, and check how a measure designed for one scenario bears on the others.

Threat Modelling. Finally, the causal pathways are still at a fairly high level of abstraction, and further work is needed to make them specific enough to trace an exact route to catastrophe. Natural directions include wargames and more precise forecasts, simulations of how specific routes might play out, and studying how the world could be made more resistant to each scenario (world hardening).

Much of this has been done before in different forms. We think however that our work can have a role in making the effort more systematic, by providing clearer reference points and targets for these discussions and investigations. We welcome criticism, suggestions and proposals for further continuations of the project.

This post was mostly not written by the authors of the original paper, who nonetheless reviewed, edited and approved it. The aim of the post is summarising and presenting the main contents of the paper at a high level of generality.
